SK2090 The finalizer can throw

A throw can leave a finalizer, where nothing catches it and the process ends.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0
SupersedesS1048

Why

An exception that escapes a finalizer is not caught anywhere. The runtime tears the process down from the finalizer thread, and the stack it prints names the finalizer queue rather than the code that put the object on it — so the one failure mode with no recovery path is also the one with the least diagnostic value. There is no try a caller can write that helps, because on that thread there is no caller.

Example

Instead of:

~Buffer() {
    Dispose(false);
}

protected virtual void Dispose(bool disposing) {
    if (_handle == 0) {
        throw new InvalidOperationException("already released");
    }
}

Write:

~Buffer() {
    Dispose(false);
}

protected virtual void Dispose(bool disposing) {
    if (_handle == 0) {
        return;
    }
}

When it does not fire

⚠ The finalizer body is almost never where the throw is, so the rule follows exactly one call hop, into a method declared on the same type whose body is in this compilation. The recall that costs is named rather than hidden: a Dispose(bool) inherited from another assembly is not followed, a throw two calls down is not followed, and a virtual member overridden by a derived type is read as the body the finalized type itself runs — which is why an abstract declaring type is skipped entirely. ⚠ The `disposing` guard is what keeps the hop honest. The disposal pattern's whole structure is if (disposing) { ... } holding the managed cleanup, which the finalizer path never enters; when the call site passes the literal false, throws that the branch condition proves unreachable are dropped, and without that every correct implementation of the pattern that throws anywhere in its managed half would be a false positive. Only an explicit throw counts — a finalizer that calls something which might throw is every finalizer ever written. A throw inside the try block of a try/catch, or inside a lambda or a local function, is not on the escaping path and is not reported. Report-only: wrapping the body in catch { } silences the rule and swallows the failure, deleting the throw deletes whatever the author meant by it, and which of the two is right is a decision about what the type owns.
